year: undated (no earlier than 2017; cited by S116, Oct 2020)
title: A test set of quadratic, binary quadratic and integer quadratic programs
contribution: A three-page description of a 1,551-instance nonconvex QP/MIQP library (246 BoxQP, 960 CBQP, 30 QSAP, 315 EIQP) that keeps and enlarges published random sets and is the test bed of S116 and S133.
problem_entry: A shared, larger test bed for nonconvex QPs and MIQPs: published random sets (BoxQP up to n = 125, EIQP up to n = 40) are kept and enlarged; no rationale for the choice of classes is given (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Keep every inherited instance and add new ones from the same generator at larger n and density: BoxQP 99 + 147 = 246, CBQP 960 unchanged, QSAP 30 without a cited source, EIQP 45 + 270 = 315 (pp. 1-3).
assumptions: Random instances only; uniform coefficient distributions on stated intervals; knobs n, density, cardinality M and coefficient interval; EIQP has one equality row, integer data, b = 15 or 20 times the sum of A_i, bounds 30/50/70, so a constant integer point is feasible (my arithmetic) (pp. 1-3).
experiments: none in the document (pp. 1-3); the set is the test bed of S116 (BARON 19.12 against six other solvers, S116 p. 23) and S133 (BARON 20.4, S133 p. 20)
positioning: Builds on five published random sets (Vandenbussche & Nemhauser 2005; Burer & Vandenbussche 2009; Burer 2010; Lima & Grossmann 2017; Billionnet, Elloumi & Lambert 2013), two of them from fellow team members Burer and Grossmann; no self-citation (p. 3).
writing: A bare data note: one subsection per class with model, size and density ranges, coefficient distributions and original vs added counts; no motivation, results or URL; a typo ('expaded', p. 1) and a degenerate interval '[-1, -1]' as printed (p. 2).
limits_future: Not stated by the authors: no reference optima, best-known bounds or difficulty data, no file format, seeds or generator code, no download location in the document itself; no future work (pp. 1-3).

method_links.note: step 5: the test bed of two BARON papers (S116, S133) released as a public library with a stand-alone description, hosted on the industrial co-author's FTP server (S133 p. 28); whether it joined BARON's development set is not stated

built on five published sets rather than a private one, but ships no certified optima, best-known bounds or difficulty data, so users can only compare relaxations by bounds and gaps against each other

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: extend inherited sets with their own generator
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: published BoxQP (99) and EIQP (45) instances kept intact and enlarged by the same distributions or class rules at larger n and density (147 and 270 new), with per-source counts, so results stay comparable with the source papers
existing candidate (S018): classes indexed by n, density, cardinality M and coefficient interval

transferable: When building a test library for a new relaxation, keep the instances earlier papers used and add new ones from the same generator at sizes beyond them, stating counts per source (99 + 147 BoxQP; 45 + 270 EIQP), so that old and new results stay comparable (pp. 1-3).

Write the library a short stand-alone note per class (model, size and density ranges, coefficient distributions, source paper) and cite it from every paper that uses the set (pp. 1-3; S116 p. 23; S133 p. 20).

For random equality-constrained integer instances, set the right-hand side from a known interior integer point (b = c times the sum of A_i with c < u_i), so that every instance is feasible by construction (pp. 2-3; the rule comes from Billionnet et al.).
coauthors: Carlos J. Nohra, Arvind U. Raghunathan

quotes.text: In the following, we describe a large collection of nonconvex problems consisting of quadratic, binary quadratic and integer quadratic programs.
This collection is an expanded version of the set of BoxQP instances generated in [2, 3, 5].

title: MINLP for regularized symbolic regression with applications to data-driven modeling of critical minerals processes
contribution: A conference poster (ACS Spring Meeting 2026) on BIC-regularized symbolic regression solved by STAR as a surrogate for a critical-minerals leaching unit: R2 near 1 on all 30 outputs and the smallest optimum deviation from 10 points, at 4-5 orders of magnitude more training time than ALAMO quadratics; the same study as the S271 deck.
problem_entry: The application question 'What data-driven techniques are the most appropriate to model and optimize critical mineral processes?' is first answered by the prior ALAMO sparse-quadratic result (Fardis et al. 2025); SR then enters as the method that assumes no model form but must be guarded against overfitting (p. 1).
key_idea: SR as a disjunctive program (Cozad 2014) solved by STAR randomized rounding of the relaxed MINLP (Sarwar 2022), with the objective changed to BIC = n_data ln(SSR/n_data) + L ln n_data, L the tree depth; each surrogate is then embedded in min f(x) s.t. h(x) = 0 over the input box (p. 1, image).
assumptions: One leaching tank (sulfuric acid and solid feed in, leach solution and solid waste out), 30 outputs; complexity = tree depth, not the number of fitted parameters of the usual BIC (my observation); input ranges, sampling, noise and the points on which R2 and parity plots are computed are not stated (p. 1).
proof_devices: n/a: no proofs (p. 1); modelling device: BIC with tree depth L as its complexity term used as the MINLP objective (p. 1, image)
experiments: star_bic vs star vs alamo_quad on one unit: training time (star_bic about 1,300 s and star about 550 s at 10 points, about 7,500 s and 4,300 s at about 50; alamo_quad near 0 s up to 1,000 points), per-output R2 (star about 0.74 on Gd and 0.62 on Y, the others near 1), a Gd parity pair, and optimum deviation (star_bic about 0.04%, star about 0.7%, alamo_quad 0.14-0.27%) (p. 1, image; approximate readings)
positioning: Places the method in MINLP symbolic regression (Cozad 2014; Sarwar 2022) and against the group's own ALAMO quadratics (Fardis et al. 2025), which had beaten lasso, ANN, kriging and RBF; no outside SR or ML method is cited on the poster (p. 1).
writing: A question-led poster: application question, prior answer, formulation, price, accuracy, optimization, conclusions; the headline 'Regularized SR prevents overfitting' is set in red without a stated train/test protocol (p. 1, image).
limits_future: Stated: training 4-5 orders of magnitude slower, doubled by BIC; SR efficient only for moderate numbers of training points; future: other model-selection criteria and complexity metrics. Not stated: no optimality bound for the chosen trees, one unit, no repeats, SR runs stop at about 50 points (p. 1).

method_links.note: an algebraic model of a simulated unit chosen by an information criterion inside an MINLP, embedded in optimization over the input box, with the price stated (4-5 orders of magnitude, doubled by BIC); the poster starts from the ALAMO sparse-quadratic verdict; same evidence as S271, count once
the SR MINLP is not solved to certified optimality: STAR rounds a relaxation randomly and no bound on the chosen tree is reported (Research Taste mark 3 not met for model selection)

surrogates judged by the deviation of their optimum and solution point from a reference optimum ('Correct solution point'); the reference is not named on the poster (the deck gives the EO optimum, S271 p. 16)

transferable: Show what regularization buys with a paired parity plot (regularized vs unregularized) for an output on which the unregularized model fails (here Gd, R2 about 0.74), next to per-output R2 for all 30 outputs (p. 1, image).

Open an applied poster with the application question, answer it with the group's earlier benchmark winner, then test the new method against that winner on the same axes: training time, R2 and optimum deviation (p. 1).

quotes.text: Regularization with BIC doubles the training time for SR.

title: The Treewidth-Convex HullTheorem and DP for Cut Generation in MINLP
contribution: A MIP 2024 poster giving an alternative DP-based proof of the bounded-treewidth LP theorem (with a TDI corollary) and a column-generation framework with DP pricing for multilinear cut generation, whose root bounds beat BARON's 20-minute lower bound by 43-67% on synthetic instances.
problem_entry: A known theorem (an unconstrained binary polynomial problem with treewidth d has an LP of size O(n2^d), Bienstock-Munoz) is re-proved, and the exponential column count of the multilinear CGLP dual of Bao et al. 2015 (one column per box vertex) is attacked (p. 1).
key_idea: Rewrite the bounded-treewidth LP as a DP (integrality, then TDI); solve the multilinear CGLP dual by column generation, whose pricing problem L(b) - pi^T b - pi_0 is an unconstrained binary problem solved by DP; add z >= ax + b when violated (p. 1).
assumptions: A multilinear intermediate over a finite box; bounded treewidth with a known tree decomposition (instances generated from one; finding one is not discussed); n = 25-30 with d = 10 (table), n = 15-20 with 40 or 80 monomials (Fig. 2) (p. 1).
proof_devices: conversion of the bounded-treewidth LP into a DP formulation to prove integrality, TDI as a corollary (p. 1; the proof is not on the poster)
column generation on the CGLP dual with an unconstrained-binary pricing problem solved by DP over the tree decomposition (p. 1)
cut z >= ax + b read from the duals of the convex-combination constraints and added if z* < ax* + b (p. 1)
experiments: CGLP time, DP vs an unexplained 'gray code' method on n = 15-20 (n = 20: under 1 s vs about 46 s with 40 monomials, about 34 s vs about 64 s with 80); root bound with the new cuts vs BARON's lower bound at 20 min on 12 example instances (n = 25-30, d = 10): better by 60.8-67.0% (unconstrained) and 43.2-50.3% (linearly constrained) after 76-184 s; BARON version and settings, the basic relaxation and optimal values not given (p. 1, table and image)
positioning: Extends BARON's multilinear-intermediate cut generation (Bao, Khajavirad, Sahinidis & Tawarmalani 2015) with the Bienstock-Munoz bounded-treewidth LP (2018); BARON is the baseline (p. 1).
writing: Summary, theorem, contribution, framework, results and conclusion on one poster; results given as 'Better by' percentages over BARON's 20-minute bound, without optimal values or solver settings (p. 1).
limits_future: Future work: integration within the branch-and-bound tree of standard solvers; also limiting: synthetic instances from known tree decompositions, one example instance per size and type, root bounds only, DP time growing steeply with 80 monomials (p. 1).

method_links.note: step 1, partial: the new cuts reported with bound and time together (76-184 s against BARON's 20-minute bound) and the separation timed against an alternative; no failure count, no library

step 3: the costly exact multilinear separation is kept and made cheaper (column generation with DP pricing over a tree decomposition) instead of being emulated by a cheaper object; numerical safety not discussed
a stand-alone prototype judged against BARON's lower bound from outside, not an on/off build inside BARON; integration into standard solvers' branch and bound is future work

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the DP that re-proves exactness of the bounded-treewidth LP is the pricing routine of the column-generation cut generator (my reading of how the poster's two halves connect)

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Transfer integer-programming devices into global optimization
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: existing candidate (s02): column generation and DP over a tree decomposition used to separate multilinear cuts
existing candidate (S018): instances generated from a known tree decomposition with n, d and number of monomials set

transferable: When a cut-generating LP has one column per box vertex, solve its dual by column generation; the pricing problem is a binary polynomial problem over the same interaction graph, so a DP over a tree decomposition prices it exactly (p. 1).
Generate test instances from a known tree decomposition, so that n and the width d can be varied separately (p. 1).
coauthors: Sourabh K Choudhary, Santanu S. Dey

quotes.text: We show that the LP can be converted into a DP formulation and hence the integrality can be proven.
Future work involves integrating this within the Branch and Bound (B&B) tree of standard solvers.
